fecund

/FEK-uhnd/ - the stress falls on FEK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fecund means fertile, producing new life or ideas in teeming abundance.

The volcanic terraces are so fecund that farmers there joke about harvesting anything they happen to drop.

Example

Grandfather's back plot shamed the whole allotment: the same seed packets everyone bought produced double there, and neighbors swore his fecund half-acre could sprout a fence post if he watered it.

Fecund reaches past 'productive' — a productive plot earns its keep, but a fecund one seems to overflow with life on its own, generating more than anyone asked of it. The word covers minds, too: a fecund mind breeds ideas the way rich soil breeds seedlings.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

prolific: Prolific counts the output: a prolific author, a prolific vine — many works, many grapes, one after another. Fecund points at the generative power behind the output, the teeming fertility that keeps producing whether anyone asks or not. A prolific writer publishes constantly; a fecund imagination breeds more ideas than could ever be written down.

bountiful: Bountiful praises what is given — a bountiful harvest, a bountiful host — generosity in the yield itself. Fecund looks earlier in the process, at the power to keep producing: soil, species, or minds teeming with new life. A bountiful table is loaded once; a fecund garden keeps loading it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

barren: produces nothing at all

sterile: incapable of supporting life or growth

Where it sits · how overflowing the yield is

productive → fruitful → fecund

productive vs. fecund: Productive stops short of fecund — a productive plot meets its quota and not much more.

fruitful vs. fecund: Fruitful stops short of fecund — a fruitful season gives a good yield, while a fecund one buries you in zucchini and volunteer seedlings.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fecund: fruitful (borrowed whole from Latin fecundus)

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: fecund came into English whole from Latin fecundus, 'fruitful.' Behind the Latin sits an ancient root meaning 'to nourish, to suckle,' but that family survives only in distant technical cousins, so the word stands alone on the page — as self-contained as a seed.

Why there's no relative to spot: Fecund arrived whole from Latin fecundus, 'fruitful.' Its ancient root — meaning 'to nourish, to suckle' — does survive, but only in remote technical words like fetus, which no longer look or feel related. With no everyday cousin to give it away, fecund must be learned on its own.

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / scientific

Fecund is the writer's and biologist's word; in everyday speech, fertile does the job. Choose fecund when you want abundance with a hint of wonder or excess — fecund soil, a fecund imagination — production that outruns anyone's plans.
